item.title: Distinct Patterns of Syntactic Errors Doubly Dissociate in Chronic Poststroke Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
The lesion correlates of syntactic deficits in aphasia remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested that distinct error types in expressive syntax may be associated with damage to different brain regions, but the specific lesion correlates of these errors have not been fully delineated. To address this gap, we analyzed spontaneous speech samples from individuals with chronic aphasia, categorizing errors into hierarchical (paragrammatic-like) and linearization (agrammatic-like) errors. Lesion-symptom mapping was conducted to identify brain regions associated with these error types. Lesion clusters in the medial superior temporal sulcus and inferior parietal lobe were associated with hierarchical errors, whereas frontal lesions, including those in the inferior and middle frontal lobe, were associated with linearization errors. These results provide support for a two-stage model of syntactic encoding, with distinct neural correlates for hierarchical and linearization processes. Our findings suggest that distinct brain regions contribute to different stages of syntactic encoding. Hierarchical processing seems to be supported by posterior temporal-parietal regions, whereas linearization seems to be supported by frontal regions. These results suggest that the diagnosis and treatment of aphasia could take into account the existence of distinct syntactic production deficits resulting from different patterns of brain damage.

item.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

item.title: Neurobehavioral correlates of changing one's mind in ADHD and OCD.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Cognitive flexibility is an executive function that allows individuals to adjust behavior in response to changing environmental demands. We assessed volitional switching under uncertainty, without rule-based learning, in the "Change Your Mind" task. Nineteen patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), 19 patients with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and matched control participants (20 per group) completed the task while undergoing a functional MRI scan. The task was a two-alternative forced choice paradigm where each stimulus was presented twice successively, with spurious feedback following the first presentation. This allowed participants the opportunity to repeat or change their response. Participants with ADHD changed their response more frequently than controls following a previously correct response, associated with reduced accuracy on the second trial. This was accompanied with smaller differences between change and repeat trials in the superior frontal gyrus, paracingulate gyrus, and frontal pole compared to controls. Participants with OCD did not differ from healthy controls in their performance but exhibited greater activity on both change and repeat trials in the pre- and postcentral gyri than controls. These results point to distinct neurobehavioral differences in patients with ADHD and OCD underlying what is often termed more broadly inflexible behavior.

item.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. Results 1) In both males and females in early affective psychosis and healthy controls, bilaterally, the frontal cortex to caudate wiring pattern deviated from a topographic organization. 2) in a right hemisphere frontal pole fiber cluster, independent of sex, we found a significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.013); 3) in a left hemisphere inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, fiber cluster, we found sex influenced the significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.0085), with the effect much greater in females (p < 0.00001) than in males (p = 0.97); and, 4) post-hoc tests showed a significant effect of diagnosis on the pattern of frontal cortex to caudate connectivity in specific subregions (ps ≤0.04). Conclusions Importantly, while the frontostriatal wiring pattern in both early affective psychosis and healthy controls deviated from a topographic organization, we found in a right hemisphere fiber cluster, independent of sex, that a significant interaction effect of diagnosis was observed on the frontal cortex to caudate connectivity pattern, whereas, in a left hemisphere fiber cluster, the effect of diagnosis on connectivity pattern was influenced by sex, showing the importance of the role of sex in brain wiring patterns in early affective psychosis.

item.title: SPARK-ICA: Guided Frequency-Resolved Dynamic Spatial ICA Reveals Fine-Scale fMRI Network Dynamics.
item.description:
Human brain mapping
Fine-scale spatiotemporal dynamics of functional brain networks are increasingly recognized as critical markers of transient connectivity and neuropsychiatric pathology. However, many existing dynamic fMRI methods primarily focus on temporal variability without explicitly resolving the spatial-frequency content of network dynamics, potentially limiting characterization of subtle, high-frequency spatial reconfigurations. To address this gap, we propose SPARK-ICA (Spatial-frequency Partitioned, Adaptive Reconstruction using Knowledge-guided ICA), a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial independent component analysis (ICA) framework that integrates NeuroMark template guidance with spatial frequency decomposition and group-level ICA of time-resolved, band-specific spatial maps. Starting from template-guided NeuroMark networks, we first estimate time-varying spatial maps using a dynamic guided ICA approach, capturing subject-specific network expression over time. Each dynamic spatial map is then decomposed into multiple spatial frequency bands using Fourier-domain spatial filtering, isolating fine- to coarse-scale spatial features at each time point. Band-specific spatial maps are subsequently concatenated and subjected to a blind group-level multi-frequency ICA, yielding a compact latent representation in which each dynamic component is characterized by distinct spatial-frequency signatures. These group-level band-resolved components are then used as references to estimate subject- and band-specific time courses and maps via spatially constrained ICA, enabling frequency-specific analysis of both long-term correlations and short-term temporal variability while preserving reproducibility across subjects. Using resting-state fMRI data from schizophrenia (SZ) patients and healthy controls (HC), we evaluated both long-term correlations and short-term variability of band-resolved dynamic time courses. For the group-level analyses, we focused on a predefined subset of NeuroMark networks with well-established involvement in SZ-related dysconnectivity. Our results reveal frequency-specific abnormalities in SZ, with enhanced long-term connectivity within sensory and subcortical networks and pronounced short-term alterations involving predominantly higher-frequency spatial components, particularly in cerebellar and subcortical systems. These findings indicate that SZ-related dysregulation is differentially expressed across spatial-frequency and temporal scales, rather than reflecting uniform dysconnectivity. Together, this framework provides a unified approach for analyzing dynamic fMRI networks across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions, extending our previous NeuroMark-DyFICA framework from a predominantly high-frequency spatial representation to an explicitly frequency-resolved characterization of dynamic network organization. By explicitly modeling spatial frequency-dependent dynamics, the proposed method provides a more resolved characterization of network alterations and offers a framework for identifying candidate markers of neuropsychiatric disorders.

item.title: Structural Brain Correlates of Bulimia Nervosa Diagnosis and Symptom Severity: A Coordinated ENIGMA Eating Disorders Working Group Analysis.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Importance Bulimia nervosa (BN) ranks second among eating disorders in both prevalence and disease burden, but its neurobiology is poorly understood. Progress has been limited by neuroimaging studies with inconsistent findings across small samples. Objective To identify reliable structural brain correlates of BN diagnosis and severity across multiple cohorts worldwide. Design, setting, and participants This case-control study used 3-dimensional T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical data. Prospective meta-analyses assessed group differences in cortical thickness (CT), surface area (SA), and subcortical volumes (SV) and associations with symptom severity. Data were analyzed between February 1, 2022, and October 1, 2025. Thirteen international sites (17 cohorts) participating in the Enhancing Neuroimaging Genetics through Meta-Analysis (ENIGMA) Eating Disorders Working Group were included, yielding a total of 369 participants with BN and 417 healthy control individuals. Main outcomes and measures Regional CT, SA, and SV extracted from T1-weighted MRI scans (uniformly preprocessed using ENIGMA-standardized pipelines and quality control procedures); binge eating severity; and compensatory behavior severity. Results Participants were all female with a mean (range) age of 23.6 (12.0-53.6) years. Relative to control individuals, the BN group had lower nucleus accumbens volume (Cohen d, -0.20; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.06) and lower cortical SA of the superior temporal (d, -0.26; 95% CI, -0.41 to -0.12) and transverse temporal cortices (d, -0.24; 95% CI, -0.38 to -0.10). We did not observe significant group differences in CT. Most differences remained significant when controlling for cohort-level variation in body mass index, illness duration, depressive symptoms, psychotropic medication use, and purging as a compensatory behavior. Binge-eating frequency was associated with lower SA of the superior temporal cortex, insula, pars orbitalis, and medial orbitofrontal, rostral middle frontal, and isthmus and posterior cingulate gyri (r value range, -0.20 to -0.14) but not CT or SV. No anatomical characteristics were associated with total compensatory behaviors. Conclusions and relevance This case-control study found that localized brain structural alterations, mostly in SA, were associated with BN and BN symptoms. These findings provide evidence implicating reward, cognitive control, interoceptive, and social cognition circuits in the pathophysiology of BN, advancing neurobiological models of a disorder with a poorly characterized brain basis.

item.title: Neural Markers of Reward Valuation and Impulsive Decision-Making in Mania Risk.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
IMPORTANCE: Mania or hypomania, the pathognomonic feature of bipolar disorder (BD), is associated with reward hypersensitivity and impulsive decision-making, but the neural mechanisms underlying these distinct behavioral facets remain unclear. Reward expectancy (RE)-associated activation in the left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (L-vlPFC) and pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) is elevated in individuals at risk of mania or hypomania, but it is unknown whether elevated activation in these regions and associations with risk-related behavioral facets reflect convergent or dissociable pathways to mania or hypomania risk or whether depression severity impacts these associations. OBJECTIVE: To test whether RE-associated L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation exhibit distinct associations with delay discounting behavior-indexing reward valuation (lower discounting) vs impulsive decision-making (higher discounting)-and whether these associations are moderated by depression severity. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: In this cross-sectional study, 2 independent samples of adults aged approximately 18 to 30 years at varying risk of mania or hypomania (142 in the discovery set and 86 in the replication set) completed a functional magnetic resonance imaging reward task and a delay discounting assessment. Major exclusion criteria included current or lifetime BD, primary psychotic disorders, neurological disorders, recent substance use disorders, systemic medical illnesses, and magnetic resonance imaging contraindications. The study took place from 2019 to 2026 at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. EXPOSURE: RE-associated L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Main outcomes were mania or hypomania risk per Mood Spectrum Self-Report-Lifetime mania score and delay discounting behavior per 27-Item Monetary Choice Questionnaire rate. Associations were tested using regression models, including moderation by depression severity. RESULTS: Across 228 individuals (discovery: mean [SD] age, 23.79 [3.32] years; 96 [67.6%] female; replication: mean [SD] age, 26.09 [3.15] years; 64 [74.4%] female), L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation were both positively associated with mania or hypomania risk in the discovery sample (l-vlPFC: β, 0.544; 95% CI, 0.440 to 0.649; z, 10.24; P < .001 and pre-SMA: β, 0.496; 95% CI, 0.341 to 0.650; z, 6.30; P < .001) and replication sample (l-vlPFC: β, 0.503; 95% CI, 0.241 to 0.765; z, 3.77; P < .001 and pre-SMA: β, 0.684; 95% CI, 0.410 to 0.957; z, 4.90; P < .001). In the discovery sample, these regions showed dissociable delay discounting associations: greater L-vlPFC activation was associated with lower discounting (β, -0.305; 95% CI, -0.561 to -0.050; P = .02), whereas greater pre-SMA activation was associated with higher discounting (β, 0.521; 95% CI, 0.146 to 0.895; P = .007). The L-vlPFC-lower discounting association replicated (β, -0.704; 95% CI, -1.400 to -0.008; P = .048). A pre-SMA activation × depression severity interaction was observed in the replication sample (β, -0.427; 95% CI, -0.792 to -0.063; P = .02), such that higher depression severity attenuated the association between elevated pre-SMA activation and higher discounting. This interaction was detectable in the discovery sample in individuals with elevated pre-SMA activation (β, -0.285; 95% CI, -0.565 to -0.005; t63 = -2.03; P = .046). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: The findings in this cross-sectional study suggest that RE-associated L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation may represent dissociable neural pathways to mania or hypomania risk. Elevated L-vlPFC activation was associated with sensitivity to reward value, whereas elevated pre-SMA activation was associated with impulsive decision-making, and this latter association was moderated by depression severity.

item.title: Neural and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety: Widespread brain network alterations, increased control costs, and visuospatial processing deficits.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
This study investigated the neural substrates and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety, which are currently incompletely understood, in N = 3,499 youth with median (IQR) age 12.0 (1.1) years (~51.0% females), from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Study. Resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, anxiety (scores and related disorder diagnoses), and neurocognitive data were analyzed. Mixed-effects regression models were used to examine associations between anxiety, brain characteristics (topological and morphometric properties, and regulatory (control) costs of intrinsic network dynamics), and cognitive outcomes. Females, older youth, and those with more parental mental health problems had higher anxiety (β = 0.04-1.15, 95% CI = [0.01, 2.18]). Higher resting-state connectivity and/or centrality (network importance) of the cerebellum, amygdala, and thalamus, and higher cerebellum-basal-ganglia-thalamus control costs were associated with higher anxiety (β = 0.04-0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.11]). In contrast, temporoparietal and frontoparietal network efficiency and resilience (robustness) were protective for social and/or generalized anxiety disorders (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 0.72-0.80, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.98]). Higher cortical thickness and/or volume of the superior temporal gyrus, pars opercularis, precentral gyrus, and putamen were associated with higher odds of generalized or social anxiety disorder (aOR = 1.28-1.44, 95% CI = [1.07, 1.78]). Finally, anxiety was associated with lower response accuracy in the Little Man Task (β = -0.05, 95% CI = [-0.09, -0.01]), and attenuated positive brain-task performance associations. These findings suggest that adolescent anxiety is associated with widespread brain alterations, especially in the cerebellum-basal ganglia-thalamus network, while the organization of frontoparietal and temporoparietal networks, which play as key role in emotion regulation and social function, is protective for anxiety disorders. It is also associated with lower visuospatial processing and alterations in the networks that support it.

item.title: Brain systems supporting the narrative self and psychopathology.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Disturbances in the narrative self are implicated across psychiatric disorders, with abnormalities in the neural systems supporting its generation and regulation constituting a transdiagnostic risk factor for mental illness. This review highlights how alterations in these brain systems underlie prevalent clinical features, including diminished, rigid, and sustained negative beliefs within the narrative self. The narrative self is framed as a higher-order construct that emerges from multiple systems, with reward, punishment, and motivational signals biasing which experiences are encoded as self-defining and which self-beliefs are reinforced over time. We discuss recent evidence demonstrating how the narrative self is supported by distributed brain networks in which subcortical inputs from the basal forebrain, habenula and mediodorsal thalamus modulate default mode network activity, with the salience, frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, and hippocampal-parahippocampal networks regulating how self-beliefs are established or updated. Adolescence is emphasized as a developmental period uniquely vulnerable to disturbances in the formation of a coherent, flexible narrative self, wherein asynchronous subcortical and cortical development and pubertal changes interact to confer risk for diminished and rigid self-beliefs. Belief-updating tasks, hierarchical computational models, and ecological momentary assessment are proposed as approaches to quantify how self-beliefs form and shift across time, linking neural signatures of the narrative self to momentary variability. We propose that treating the narrative self as a primary level of explanation for psychopathology positions it as a testable target for future neuroimaging research, providing a clearer bridge from self-referential cognition to interventions in daily life.

item.title: The dual future of OPM-MEG: Clinical translation and naturalistic neuroscience.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) has moved beyond proof of principle. The decisive question is no longer whether cryogen-free sensors can detect neuromagnetic fields from the human brain with sufficient sensitivity, but whether complete systems can deliver clinical decision value and interpretable recordings during more naturalistic behaviour. Here we argue that OPM-MEG is developing along two partly overlapping trajectories. One is clinical translation, where usefulness depends more on reliable workflows, calibrated source localisation, auditable quality control, and empirical evidence for improved diagnostic or treatment decisions. The other is naturalistic neuroscience, where wearable measurement can connect neural dynamics to movement, action, and social behaviour without conflating neural activity with movement-related artefacts. Both trajectories depend on a shared engineering stack including magnetic field control, dense spatial sampling, accurate calibration, integrated electronics, artefact suppression, participant comfort, and synchronised behavioural measurement. The next stage of OPM-MEG should be evaluated by clinical utility in specific patient groups, statistically identifiable neural dynamics in behaviourally rich settings, and sufficient system detail for replication across systems and sites.

item.title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth.
item.description:
Science (New York, N.Y.)
Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development-its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

item.title: The amygdaloid complex: from morphology to neurodegeneration.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
The amygdaloid complex is one of the most structurally and functionally heterogeneous regions of the mammalian brain, acting as an integrative node between sensory, mnemonic and visceral systems. It comprises a set of subnuclei whose cytoarchitectural differentiation, neurochemical profiles and anatomical boundaries have been debated since the earliest descriptions. This heterogeneity is established during ontogenetic development, assembling progenitors from pallial and subpallial domains, and preoptic and hypothalamic territories, resulting in a highly connected network. Maturation is not complete at birth, the amygdala changes through childhood and adolescence, leaving a protracted window of environmental sensitivity. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have added a molecular layer to this framework, resolving populations that no single marker separates, and set explicit limits on the resolution at which rodent-derived subdivisions can be transferred to the human amygdala. Together these levels of description provide a structural framework for understanding its functions, which include emotional regulation and conditioned fear, social and sexual behaviours, decision-making, reward and punishment processing, empathy and memory modulation. Cross-species comparison reveals further variation, particularly the expansion of the basolateral complex in primates and the redistribution of neurons towards the lateral nucleus in humans. In summary, the amygdala acts as a densely connected hub with a broad role not only in physiological and psychological health but also in disease states; indeed, the amygdala is affected early in several neurodegenerative disorders, and in some (notably limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy and argyrophilic grain disease) it is among the first regions in which pathology is detected.
